    #62346. How Often Do You Need To Scrub The Do Not Call List? The 31-Day Rule Explained

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1043 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    How Often Do You Need To Scrub The Do Not Call List? The 31-Day Rule Explained

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1043 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Phil Portman is a serial entrepreneur and the Founder & CEO of Textdrip — a small business SMS marketing tool to automate SMS campaigns.
    • ​I see businesses repeatedly making the same mistake: They scrub their contact list once and then keep calling and texting from that list for months.
    • Recent findings suggest that after years of experience working in a regulated industry, I’m sure about one thing: Businesses rarely fail because the rules are unclear.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Phil Portman is a serial entrepreneur and the Founder & CEO of Textdrip — a small business SMS marketing tool to automate SMS campaigns.

    ​I see businesses repeatedly making the same mistake: They scrub their contact list once and then keep calling and texting from that list for months. That’s a risky habit, because every day newly introduced numbers join the Do Not Call Registry. A list that was clean in January can be full of problems by March.

    Recent findings suggest that after years of experience working in a regulated industry, I’m sure about one thing: Businesses rarely fail because the rules are unclear. They fail because their processes break down in practice. The Do Not Call rules are a crystal-clear example of this.

    In a recent development, how often do you have to scrub the Do Not Call (DNC) list? Every 31 days. To keep safe harbor protection, you need to scrub against a version of the registry that is no more than 31 days old. In practice, that means every month.

    According to recent reports, the National Do Not Call Registry is run by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC). It lets people add their personal phone numbers to a list that tells telemarketers to stop contacting them. It exists to protect consumers who don’t want sales calls. It covers personal numbers, such as home and mobile lines. It doesn’t cover business-to-business calls to a company line. Knowing this difference helps you decide which numbers need a check.

    Many teams assume it only covers voice calls, but it doesn’t. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) treats text messages as calls, so the same protections apply to SMS marketing. If you text prospects, those numbers also need a DNC check.

    It has been revealed that state lists exist as well. Some states keep their own Do Not Call lists, and some, such as Florida and Texas, have stricter rules than the federal registry. If you contact people in several states, you need to check each state’s rules before you launch.

    Industry observers note that some calls are exempt, such as those to people who gave written permission or have an established business relationship with you. Even then, you must honor opt-out requests.

    Sources indicate that to qualify for safe harbor under FTC and FCC regulations, telemarketers must scrub their list against the National DNC Registry. Every call must be made using a registry version downloaded no more than 31 days earlier. Simply put, you must rescrub every month. If it’s day 32, you’re already at risk.

    Recent findings suggest that suppose you scrubbed a list on the first of the month. On the 20th, a prospect joins the registry. Your team keeps working that same list. Any call made after day 31 relies on an outdated version. Many teams scrub only when they upload fresh leads. This sounds fine, but a campaign can run for weeks, and a number can join the registry halfway through. If you keep contacting that number, you’re working from outdated data.

    It has been revealed that safe harbor is a defense that protects a business when a call goes out by mistake. But it only applies if you had a working process in place before the mistake happened. A written policy that nobody reads or follows won’t help. Training without a current list won’t help either.

    The FCC rule lists what a DNC safe harbor process needs:.

    • Written Do Not Call procedures.

    • Staff trained on those procedures.

    • An internal Do Not Call list that is kept up to date.

    • Registry access used to scrub within the 31-day window.

    • Logs (records) showing when each scrub happened.

    Record-keeping is a common gap. Without records, you have no safe harbor, even if the scrub did happen. If a regulator or a lawyer asks for proof, saying “we did it” won’t be enough. You need proof (dates and logs).

    Do Not Call violations get expensive quickly. Under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act (TCPA), a consumer can sue for $500 per violation. If the violation was willful or knowing, a court can raise that to $1,500 per violation. A consumer generally must receive more than one call from the same business within 12 months to bring a DNC claim.

    It has been revealed that some of these claims are filed as class actions. One outdated list can hold thousands of people, and each one may have a claim. A small gap in your process can turn into a very large bill. Legal fees and settlements add to that, along with damage to your business reputation.

    I lead a firm in a regulated industry, so I think about this often. Compliance works best when it is practiced as a routine instead of an event. We built Landline Remover to help teams make scrubbing a routine.

    In a recent development, 1. Scrub every time you upload leads, not just on launch day.

    Sources indicate that 2. Rescrub active lists monthly, ideally a few days before the 31-day window closes.

    Recent findings suggest that 3. Check your internal list and the national list together. Your internal do-not-call list holds people who told you directly to stop. The registry doesn’t know about them. Both lists matter.

    According to recent reports, 4. Check reassigned numbers. Numbers change owners. The FCC’s reassigned numbers database can tell you whether a number has changed hands since you got consent.

    Industry observers note that 5. Log every scrub with the date. That log is your proof if a court or regulator asks.

    6. Automate the scrubbing process so it doesn’t depend on memory.

    It has been revealed that do Not Call compliance is a monthly habit, not a one-time task. The rule is simple: scrub within 31 days, every time.

    Recent findings suggest that DNC scrubbing alone can’t protect a business. You need to keep proof that you followed the rule. Scrubbing only protects you if you can prove it. So build a regular scrubbing habit and keep the records. Remember that regulators don’t just look at your efforts—they ask for evidence.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By David Dierking – Nov 20, 2026 at 4:45PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Vanguard S&P 500 ETF ›.

    At one point in 2025, the S&P 500 (^GSPC -3.70%) fell 19% below its high. It still finished the year up 16%.

    In 2020, the index dropped by nearly 35% during the COVID pandemic. It also closed out the full calendar year with a gain of 16%.

    In 2026, stocks are sliding again. Right now, the S&P 500 sits about 6% below its all-time high, but the Nasdaq-100 is down nearly 13%.

    Recent findings suggest that I don't tell you this to suggest that U.S. stocks are poised for a rapid recovery like they experienced earlier this decade. It's to tell you that episodes like this are part of the experience when investing in stocks.

    Recent findings suggest that if you own the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -3.42%), here's the one thing I'd tell you right now. These declines are no doubt painful, but they're the price of admission when accumulating long-term wealth.

    Sources indicate that here's an interesting bit of stock market trivia. Since 1980, the average intra-year drop in the S&P 500 has been 14.2%. But despite this, the S&P 500 has produced a positive calendar-year return in 35 of those 46 years.

    In a recent development, in other words, market corrections are a normal and regular occurrence for the S&P 500. But so are the recoveries from them. And the fact remains that stocks spend much more time rising than they do falling. The short-term losses are part of the path to long-term gains.

    One of the most underrated moves an investor can make is making no move at all.

    Sources indicate that when stock prices are falling, many people rush to sell their stocks, fearing that more losses are on the way. They may say something like they're going to wait for things to get "better" before they get back in.

    There are a couple of things wrong with that thinking.

    First, selling stocks after they've fallen only locks in the loss. It doesn't erase it. Second, stock market rebounds are often well underway by the time investors feel that things have gotten "better.".

    Sources indicate that the sum total of these actions means that a lot of folks lock in the loss, miss out on the rebound, and end up damaging their long-term returns. If the S&P 500's long-term annualized return is around 10%, the average investor usually ends up getting less than that.

    In a recent development, that's why the one thing I like to tell investors is: Get used to the stock market's volatility. It's normal and it's a daily occurrence. Corrections of 10% or more are fairly frequent and should be expected from time to time. It's how you handle them that makes the difference. If you can buy and hold instead of giving in to the temptation to sell, you have a better chance of reaching your financial goals.

    Industry News: Your Employees’ Personal AI Agents Are Becoming Your Security Problem

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1027 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • David Goldschlag is co-founder and CEO of Aembit, an identity control plane for AI agents.
    • ​Ahead of an vital client meeting, a sales representative connects their personal AI agent to tech giant email and files.
    • Personal AI agents, including Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots and Google’s Gemini Spark, are software assistants that can carry out routine tasks across connected services and continue working between conversations.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    David Goldschlag is co-founder and CEO of Aembit, an identity control plane for AI agents.

    ​Ahead of an vital client meeting, a sales representative connects their personal AI agent to tech giant email and files. The setup takes minutes and allows the employee to arrive prepared with considerably less effort, but that well-meaning shortcut may carry risks the rep never considered.

    Personal AI agents, including Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots and Google’s Gemini Spark, are software assistants that can carry out routine tasks across connected services and continue working between conversations. It is early, and there is little data yet on how often employees connect these personal assistants to tech giant accounts. But if the first numbers are any indication, the habit is forming quickly. Meta stated Muse passed 10 million accounts within roughly six weeks of launch, and a Menlo Ventures survey found that 32% of U.S. adults who use AI have already let it act on their behalf without final sign-off.

    Industry observers note that for security leaders who remember the first requests to connect personal smartphones to company email, the arrival of these agentic deputies has a familiar feel. Employees found something useful and expected to use it, while IT and security were left to reconcile that enthusiasm with responsibility for company data.

    It has been revealed that bring-your-own-device (BYOD) policies and years of “shadow IT” disputes established an enduring reality: The rank and file would have a say in the technology they used. But the analogy has limits in the AI era. Traditional software generally follows predefined workflows, while an agent can choose which tools to use and which steps to take in carrying out an employee’s request, without the employee directing each action.

    According to recent reports, permissions granted with little consideration during setup can later support a series of actions the employee never specifically contemplated. For CISOs, the difficulty is deciding how much authority should accompany that discretion and how to enforce those limits once an AI assistant begins working.

    In a recent development, consider the employee preparing for the customer meeting. The request of their agent sounds innocuous: Review recent correspondence, find the relevant account documents and prepare a briefing.

    Yet the permissions available during setup may cover far more information than this assignment requires. Depending on the connection, the agent may receive access to a mailbox containing correspondence with hundreds of customers, along with internal discussions unrelated to the meeting.

    Recent findings suggest that suppose the employee also asks the agent to prepare and send an external follow-up. An internal document contains useful background, including an unannounced pricing change. The agent could incorporate that information into a customer message because it appears relevant to the assignment. Every connection involved might be permitted, even though the resulting disclosure was never intended. Read-only access offers limited reassurance if the agent can send what it reads through another service.

    Requiring employee approval before an agent receives access provides another safeguard, but its value depends on what the employee can reasonably assess. A consent screen can describe the permissions being requested without making clear how an agent could use them together. The employee may approve those permissions without anticipating the disclosure described above.

    Industry observers note that company policy must establish which resources an assistant may access and which actions require further review. Employees should understand their responsibilities, but connecting an agent should not leave them to determine how much authority the company is willing to delegate.

    The following practices can help security leaders establish those boundaries while giving employees a practical way to use personal AI agents.

    Verify that records identify which agent acted and whose authority it used. Logs that name only the employee may leave investigators unable to distinguish direct actions from those taken by an agent.

    Establish which accounts and resources it can access, whether it can act in the background and how the provider handles credentials and retrieved data. Approval of an assistant should not imply approval of every connection it supports.

    Where controls permit, restrict access to relevant resources and separate retrieval permissions from permission to publish or send. Enforce those limits at runtime, when the agent requests access. If a service offers only broad access, weigh that limitation in the approval decision.

    Reserve employees’ attention for consequential decisions. Before an external message is sent, for example, let them review its recipients, attachments and exact content, with another review required if material details change.

    It has been revealed that ensure security can revoke an agent’s access without disabling the employee’s account. This gives security teams a way to intervene when an agent needs to be stopped. Here, that means access revocation: withdrawing the agent’s ability to use connected systems. Cutting off access, however, does not necessarily terminate the agent’s process.

    In a recent development, test it against background activity and previously issued credentials, and measure how long it takes for subsequent requests to fail. Depending on the implementation, previously issued access tokens may remain usable until they expire, or a revocation decision may take time to reach every system involved. Incident procedures should account for the behavior observed in testing, including any additional steps required to contain ongoing activity.​​​.

    These practices also expose limitations that a policy document alone cannot resolve. If a provider cannot support sufficiently narrow access or useful audit records, the company may need to restrict the information available to that agent or decline the connection.​.

    The BYOD experience offers a useful lesson about AI adoption. Employees’ preferences can influence manufacturer technology decisions long before a formal policy catches up. Security leaders should take seriously the reasons people want personal agents, including the convenience of using a tool they already know.

    Sources indicate that A workable policy should give employees a clear route to request access, explain which uses are permitted and offer alternatives when a requested connection grants more authority than the business can accept. Security teams, in turn, need evidence that the agreed restrictions hold during actual use.​​​.

    The Next Software Revolution After AI Is Efficiency

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Itamar Syn-Hershko, Founder of NeverBlink AI and BigData Boutique, helps companies confidently operate and optimize data platforms at scale.
    • For decades, we’ve made software easier to write, even when it meant making it more expensive to run.​.
    • We introduced programming languages, frameworks and layers of abstraction that allowed developers to move faster.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Itamar Syn-Hershko, Founder of NeverBlink AI and BigData Boutique, helps companies confidently operate and optimize data platforms at scale.

    For decades, we’ve made software easier to write, even when it meant making it more expensive to run.​.

    We introduced programming languages, frameworks and layers of abstraction that allowed developers to move faster. Along the way, we accepted higher memory consumption, more CPU usage and increasingly complex infrastructure.​.

    For the most part, this made sense. Developers were expensive, hardware kept getting cheaper and getting products to market swiftly was often more important than squeezing the most out of every server.​.

    I think we’re approaching a point where that trade-off no longer makes sense.​.

    Sources indicate that AI is changing the cost of writing software, while the growing demand for computing resources is making efficiency more vital than it has been in years. Together, these forces could change not just how we build software but also the economics of the entire software industry.​.

    Recent findings suggest that take Java, for example. Much of its success came from making developers more productive. Automatic memory management, a rich ecosystem and portability made it easier to build and maintain complex applications without worrying about many of the details involved in lower-level programming.​.

    Industry observers note that the trade-off was additional runtime overhead. Garbage collection, managed memory and abstraction layers can require considerably more resources than a carefully optimized native implementation.​.

    According to recent reports, this was often a perfectly reasonable compromise. If using Java saved months of engineering work, spending a little more on servers was easy to justify.​.

    But what happens when AI can write, maintain and optimize complex C++ or Rust code at a fraction of the previous engineering cost?​ We should start questioning whether some of the abstractions we’ve relied on for decades are still worth their price.​.

    I’m not suggesting we rewrite every Java application in assembly. There are good reasons to use managed languages, including their mature tooling, ecosystems and safety characteristics. AI-generated code also introduces its own risks and still needs careful review.​.

    But the argument that lower-level programming is too expensive or complicated to justify is becoming much weaker.​.

    ​At the same time, the infrastructure side of the equation is changing.​.

    Recent findings suggest that AI is creating enormous demand for computing capacity, memory, electricity and data center space. The International Energy Agency projects that global data center electricity consumption will roughly double by 2030.​.

    We cannot keep solving every software performance problem by adding more hardware. At some point, the availability and cost of that hardware become serious constraints.​.

    There’s also growing pressure to make software cheaper.​.

    Sources indicate that AI is already reducing the time and effort involved in producing software, and we should expect some of those savings to reach customers. As it becomes cheaper to build competing products, companies will find it harder to justify high prices based on development costs alone.​.

    In a recent development, this puts infrastructure efficiency at the center of the conversation. If two products offer comparable functionality but one requires a fraction of the hardware to operate, the difference can be substantial. The more efficient product can offer lower prices, better margins or both.​.

    ​Search engines and databases are good places to look for early examples.

    According to recent reports, ​Traditional search architectures (Lucene-based especially, such as Elasticsearch and OpenSearch) often require continuously provisioned compute resources and substantial memory to maintain indexes and deliver low-latency queries. This can make infrastructure costs difficult to align with fluctuating workloads.​.

    It has been revealed that ​Companies such as turbopuffer and WarpSearch are challenging those assumptions. Both use an object-storage-first architecture for vector and full-text search, reducing the need to keep large indexes on expensive infrastructure. A Google Cloud case study reports search and storage cost reductions of 90% for its approach.

    ​There are examples outside search as well, including ClickHouse, Neon, Bun and more.

    ​These products aren’t necessarily the result of AI-assisted development. Many of their innovations started before today’s coding agents became widely available.

    ​What interests me is what happens when the engineering effort required to build systems like these drops dramatically.

    ​For engineering leaders, this should change how we evaluate technology choices.

    In a recent development, ​We spend a lot of time measuring developer productivity, feature delivery and time to market. We should be paying just as much attention to what our software costs to operate.

    Industry observers note that ​That starts with measuring actual resource consumption. Cost per query, cost per transaction, memory per workload and CPU utilization are not just infrastructure metrics. They directly affect the economics of the product.

    Sources indicate that ​It also means questioning architectural decisions we’ve come to accept. Does that service really need to run continuously? Does that dataset need to stay in memory? Are we using the right algorithms and data structures? Could a more efficient implementation eliminate entire servers?

    ​And perhaps most importantly, we should be using AI for more than producing code faster.

    ​AI can help investigate performance bottlenecks, evaluate alternative algorithms, rewrite expensive components and explore lower-level implementations that would previously have required too much engineering effort.

    It has been revealed that ​There are still trade-offs. Reliability, security, correctness and maintainability matter. An implementation that saves 20% in CPU costs but introduces serious operational risks is hardly an improvement.

    ​The point is that we now have more ways to pursue efficiency without paying the same development cost we once did.

    ​I expect we’ll see more companies challenge established software categories by building products that achieve similar results with much less infrastructure.

    It has been revealed that ​Some will use better algorithms. Others will rethink storage architectures, eliminate unnecessary compute or replace expensive runtime components. AI will make many of these approaches easier to implement.

    It has been revealed that ​For established software vendors, this creates a real challenge. Their existing architectures may have been designed around assumptions that no longer hold, while newer competitors have the freedom to start from scratch.

    ​For customers, it should eventually mean more capable software at lower prices.

    ​We’ve spent decades making software easier and cheaper to write and accepting the infrastructure overhead that came with it.

    ​Now that writing software is becoming cheaper, it’s time to focus on making it cheaper to run.

    Yochai Corem is GM of Exposure Management at Check Point Software.

    Organizations have more asset data than ever, but turning that data into a reliable view of what they own, operate and expose remains difficult.

    Sources indicate that A server appears in three tools with different identifiers. A cloud workload has an owner who has left the business. A forgotten website remains online after the campaign that funded it has ended. Each leaves security teams with information they still have to investigate before they can act.

    According to recent reports, security leaders should judge asset visibility by how reliably it supports a decision. A useful inventory helps teams establish what an asset does, who is responsible for it, how it is protected and what should happen when a problem appears.

    Several familiar assumptions prevent organizations from reaching that standard.

    An incomplete configuration management database (CMDB) should prompt a review of how records are created, updated and retired.

    Recent findings suggest that start by defining its purpose. The CMDB should record the systems, services and dependencies needed to manage business operations, with accountable owners and lifecycle status. Detailed security telemetry can remain in specialist systems, linked through reliable identifiers. An impersonating website belongs in an external threat register connected to the affected brand.

    Recent findings suggest that then identify which sources can reveal missing records. Cloud platforms, endpoint management, identity providers, vulnerability scanners and procurement systems can each expose inconsistencies. Buying a service should trigger registration; retiring it should trigger checks that access, infrastructure and records have been removed.

    Recent findings suggest that reconciliation should reflect the pace of change. I would set a daily reconciliation target for cloud and endpoint feeds; use deployment and retirement events to trigger updates; and review unresolved discrepancies weekly. Quarterly ownership reviews can supplement those checks.

    Sources indicate that an asset without an owner needs an interim accountable team and an escalation deadline. “Unknown” should describe an investigation in progress.

    The modern attack surface spans internal infrastructure, cloud workloads, software as a service (SaaS), internet-facing systems, supplier connections and the organization’s broader digital presence.

    According to recent reports, those categories need different forms of accountability. Infrastructure teams may manage servers, cloud teams manage workloads and business application owners sponsor SaaS services. Marketing or regional teams may control domains and social accounts. Supplier relationships require a business sponsor alongside technical oversight.

    Security should establish a review and response process across those boundaries. A newly discovered domain needs ownership verification and an assessment of what it hosts. An unfamiliar SaaS service needs checks on its customers, data and access. A fraudulent social account needs investigation and a disruption process.

    According to recent reports, review frequency should follow exposure and change, with continuous discovery where practical and scheduled reviews for ownership, supplier access and dormant services. This broader scope aligns with the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s (NIST) inclusion of hardware, software, services and supplier services in asset management.

    Leaders can test this assumption by following a newly discovered asset through the security process.

    Industry observers note that does discovery trigger checks for required endpoint protection, vulnerability scanning and an accountable owner? Does an unmanaged internet-facing system reach someone authorized to restrict or remove it? Can the organization confirm that the resulting action occurred?

    These outcomes show whether visibility operates as a security control. The Center for Internet Security’s (CIS) Control 1 connects inventory management with identifying and addressing unauthorized or unmanaged assets.

    In a recent development, useful measures include the time taken to assign ownership, the proportion of applicable assets covered by required controls and the age of unresolved discrepancies. A growing inventory count provides little reassurance when newly discovered systems remain unmanaged.

    Additional tools introduce additional records, each with its own identifiers, timestamps and assumptions.

    Effective reconciliation requires explicit rules. Stable cloud resource identifiers or device identifiers should take precedence over an Internet Protocol (IP) address that may change or be reused. Records need source and freshness information so teams can distinguish a current observation from a stale entry.

    Organizations also need rules for conflicting fields. The identity system may establish who uses a device, while a service registry identifies the team accountable for the application it supports. Those relationships should remain distinguishable.

    It has been revealed that cyber asset attack surface management (CAASM) can support this work. Organizations can also improve CMDB integrations, use cloud asset inventories and service catalogs, or build reconciliation workflows in their existing data platforms. The operational requirements remain consistent: reliable matching, clear authority for each field and a process for resolving exceptions.

    Discovery should initiate a decision about management, protection or retirement.

    Sources indicate that A forgotten website needs an owner to confirm whether it still serves a business purpose. A vulnerable application needs assessment of its exposure, dependencies and operational constraints before a response is selected.

    That decision should remain traceable through completion. If a service is retired, verify that it is no longer reachable. If a security control is applied, confirm that it covers the intended asset. Updating the inventory should accompany the operational change.

    This ongoing connection between asset information and action also underpins continuous threat exposure management (CTEM).

    CTEM depends on this discipline throughout scoping, discovery, prioritization, validation and mobilization.

    Recent findings suggest that an unknown asset cannot enter the prioritization process. A known asset without business context is difficult to rank. Missing dependencies weaken assessments of attack paths and change impact. An unknown owner delays action, while stale records undermine confirmation that an exposure has been reduced.

    CAASM and external attack surface management (EASM) can support these stages by reconciling internal records and discovering internet-facing assets. Their value depends on the ownership, decision rules and response processes surrounding them.

    Security leaders should expect asset visibility to connect discovery with accountable action. Every significant asset needs enough current context for someone to determine its protection requirements, address its exposures and verify the result. That is how a reliable inventory helps reduce the opportunities available to an attacker.​.

    According to recent reports, forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

    SpaceX Aims to Spend $2.8 Billion on Gas Turbines. Here’s What That Much Natural Gas Demand Means for Pipeline Investors.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (769 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that when SpaceX (SPCX -7.69%) went public in June, it disclosed $2.8 billion in purchase commitments for gas turbines and related equipment in its IPO prospectus.
    • Recent findings suggest that that massive investment in behind-the-meter (BTM) natural gas connections, which generate electricity on the customer's side of the electric meter rather than going through an energy provider, is a bright green flag for the natural gas market.
    • Sources indicate that an easy way to profit from that secular trend is through midstream pipeline companies, which deliver the natural gas to those data centers.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Leo Sun – Nov 20, 2026 at 4:55PM EST.

    Industry observers note that when SpaceX (SPCX -7.69%) went public in June, it disclosed $2.8 billion in purchase commitments for gas turbines and related equipment in its IPO prospectus. SpaceX is purchasing those turbines to power its own data centers and factories.

    Recent findings suggest that that massive investment in behind-the-meter (BTM) natural gas connections, which generate electricity on the customer's side of the electric meter rather than going through an energy provider, is a bright green flag for the natural gas market. U.S. data centers already generate over 40% of their electricity from natural gas, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). That percentage could continue to rise as the cloud and AI markets expand.

    Sources indicate that an easy way to profit from that secular trend is through midstream pipeline companies, which deliver the natural gas to those data centers. Pipeline operators charge companies "tolls" to use their infrastructure, so they're well-insulated from volatile commodity prices. Instead, they simply need the resources to keep flowing through their pipes to generate stable profits. Most pipeline companies also return lots of cash to their investors through high dividends and distributions.

    Recent findings suggest that as demand for natural gas rises, pipeline companies will need to expand their infrastructure to handle the increased volumes. Those investments could compress their near-term margins, but they'll support their long-term growth. Let's see which of these pipeline operators will benefit the most from the rapid growth of the cloud infrastructure and AI data center markets.

    It has been revealed that the Williams Companies (WMB -2.75%) operates more than 32,000 miles of pipeline across 24 states. It owns Transco, the largest natural gas pipeline in the U.S., which connects the Gulf Coast to the Atlantic seaboard. Its pipelines handle roughly a third of all natural gas produced in the United States.

    NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

    Unlike more diversified pipeline companies, Williams generates most of its revenue by gathering, processing, storing, and transporting natural gas. A smaller percentage of revenue comes from natural gas liquids (NGLs), crude oil handling services, and electricity generation.

    It has been revealed that from 2025 to 2028, analysts expect Williams' EPS to grow at a 12% CAGR. It still looks reasonably valued at 26 times next year's earnings, and it could command an even higher valuation if the data center market heats up again.

    Industry observers note that williams has raised its dividend annually over the past nine years, and it's paid continuous dividends for the past 52 years. It presently pays a forward yield of 3.2%, and its low payout ratio of 82% gives it ample room for future dividend hikes.

    Energy Transfer (ET -2.62%) operates more than 140,000 miles of pipeline across 44 states. It transports crude oil, natural gas, natural gas liquids (NGLs), and other refined products through its pipelines. It also exports NGLs through its marine export terminals.

    TXSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

    Energy Transfer's pipelines transport about 30% of the natural gas produced in the United States. It generates only approximately 40% of its adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) from natural gas, which makes it less of a direct play on natural gas than Williams. Still, Energy Transfer is more exposed to that market than many of its peers.

    Industry observers note that unlike Williams, which operates as a traditional corporation, Energy Transfer is a master limited partnership (MLP) that treats its investors as partners rather than shareholders. MLPs pay distributions -- much of which are classified as a "return of capital" for more tax-efficient returns -- rather than traditional dividends. That strategy enables it to pay a high forward yield of 7.2%, but its investors must file an additional K-1 form (for MLPs) with their taxes each year.

    It has been revealed that from 2025 to 2028, analysts expect Energy Transfer's earnings per unit (EPU) to grow at a 13% CAGR. It trades at just 12 times next's year's EPU, and that low valuation should limit its downside even if the cloud and AI markets cool off over the next few years.

    Breaking: Now what? Colts should have traded Daniel Jones when they had the chance

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1194 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yahoo

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Here's the Daniel Jones timeline for the past eight months — and stick with us, because it's a wild ride.
    • The Colts signed Jones to the largest two-year contract in NFL history despite coming off Achilles surgery a few months earlier.
    • The Colts kept Jones as their starter, without any new competition, this season.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Here's the Daniel Jones timeline for the past eight months — and stick with us, because it's a wild ride.

    The Colts signed Jones to the largest two-year contract in NFL history despite coming off Achilles surgery a few months earlier.

    The Colts kept Jones as their starter, without any new competition, this season.

    The Colts continued to put Jones as QB1 while he struggled, throwing interceptions in 10 of his 11 starts.

    It has been revealed that the Colts reportedly listened to trade offers for their starting QB prior to the Nov. 10 trade deadline before ultimately passing.

    The Colts started Jones in Thursday's blowout loss to the Texans.

    The Colts released Jones on Friday.

    Whew. Caught up? Good. Now consider: Cutting Jones will cost the team nearly $15 million in dead salary-cap money, plus another $35 million for next year.

    Recent findings suggest that friday's move was nothing short of a stunner, if only from a financial standpoint. From a football standpoint, the Colts couldn't justify keeping him as the starter? Cutting him now, knowing what a hit they'd take? It almost feels personal at this point.

    Colts head coach Shane Steichen clearly had enough of him Thursday night. The speculation on why Steichen hadn't gone to Anthony Richardson Sr. sooner was that the coach might have trusted Richardson even less.

    In a recent development, steichen might also be in self-preservation mode, trying to hold together a ship that was partially stripped before the trade deadline and already in rough shape before that. But assuming Steichen didn't reach his breaking point during Thursday's game, why did the Colts wait to get rid of him?

    Sources indicate that and not only for nothing. It actually cost the Colts money and flexibility to release him now. It doesn't get much uglier than that.

    Daniel Jones' run with the Colts ends after 24 starts in which Indianapolis went 11-13.

    There have been credible reports that multiple teams inquired about Jones' availability before the trade deadline, including the Ravens and Vikings. Others might also have checked in on him. The Colts held firm. The Ravens got Jacoby Brissett and the Vikings landed Kirk Cousins.

    Recent findings suggest that this feels like a major missed opportunity. By releasing Jones, the Colts got nothing and made their situation worse. Even with the potential return of a Day 3 draft pick and a slightly better impact on their salary cap, the Colts passed.

    Recent findings suggest that it should be noted that the Vikings feel great about Cousins, and it's possible that their interest in Jones was more of a fallback option. The Ravens? Brissett's numbers over the past two seasons have been slightly better, so it's fair to say that they might have preferred the QB they ended up with.

    But any potential interest in Jones should have been met with a take-him-off-our-hands type of offer — the kind a team couldn't turn down. Someone is going to sign him here in the coming days, and given all the QB injuries around the league, it wouldn't be a stunner to see Jones start a game at some point this season.

    It has been revealed that the Colts were more than willing to part with other assets prior to the deadline, including DeForest Buckner, Quenton Nelson and Josh Downs. They listened to offers for Jones and Jonathan Taylor but ended up keeping both. Taylor had 11 carries for 21 yards and four catches for six yards on Thursday. Jones struggled and was cut. Little of this makes sense.

    In a recent development, when general manager Chris Ballard was fired midseason and replaced by interim GM Ed Dodds, it felt like an opportunity for Dodds to earn the full-time job by starting the process of replenishing the Colts' draft pool. They've done that, but they've also thrown away large chunks of meat still on the bone.

    Dodds was dealt a tough hand (one he helped put together, for what it's worth), but it's arguable he has played it poorly — unless Jones' release was mandated from on high. That's possible. If it's true, the Colts' situation is even uglier than it appears.

    Industry observers note that since Andrew Luck's shocking retirement in August 2019, the Colts have started 12 different quarterbacks. Jones' 24 starts were the most from that group in that span, but it's highly likely some fresh names are added to the list next season. This franchise is starting to become synonymous with QB instability, and after two decades of having Peyton Manning and Luck, that's a bitter pill to swallow.

    Recent findings suggest that the remaining options on the roster this season are Richardson and Riley Leonard. The Colts don't appear to have great belief in either one. They declined the fifth-year option on Richardson's rookie deal, making him a free agent this spring, and have been reluctant to give him much of a shot prior to now. Leonard was last seen in last year's Week 18 start and hasn't played a snap in 2026.

    The assumption is that Richardson will play elsewhere next season. He certainly has a chance to rewrite his story in Indy as Jones' replacement, but whatever he does down the stretch will likely serve as an audition for his next stop. Leonard could be back in 2027, but it's unlikely he'd be anything higher than a backup to start next season.

    The Colts could have waited until the offseason and made Jones a post-June 1 cut, with far less of a salary-cap footprint. The question of whether to keep Jones is settled, but the problems are only starting.

    The Sauce Gardner trade cost them next year's first-round draft pick, and though the pre-deadline trades netted them some Day 2 and 3 ammunition over the next two years, it still makes acquiring a quarterback tougher come springtime.

    Industry observers note that the Colts can still move into the bottom of Round 1 for a quarterback in next spring's draft. But will there be a viable starting candidate available in that range? What was thought to be a banner QB crop in the 2027 NFL Draft is turning into more of a grab-bag situation, depending on which underclassmen declare.

    It has been revealed that perhaps an unexpected veteran or two could hit the market. The veteran route feels more likely now, at least from an immediate-starter perspective. But will there be starting-quality options? That hope feels dubious now. Kyler Murray, Geno Smith and Deshaun Watson are the caliber of names that could be options. Do any of them elevate this team or give the Colts much more than a bridge option?

    You can forget about trading for Lamar Jackson. The Colts don't have the assets to compete. That holds true for any other potential starting QB who could be available via trade.

    In a recent development, the pathways to salvation appear quite limited. The head coach appears to be on thin ice. The Colts sunk major money into Taylor and Alec Pierce this offseason but have little to show for it.

    In short, the whole situation is a hot mess.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • By Sara Appino – Updated Nov 20, 2026 at 4:57PM EST.
    • 10 stocks we like better than Credo Technology Group ›.
    • Industry observers note that the race for faster data processing is pushing infrastructure to its limits, forcing a choice between specialized connectivity and massive storage.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Sara Appino – Updated Nov 20, 2026 at 4:57PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Credo Technology Group ›.

    Industry observers note that the race for faster data processing is pushing infrastructure to its limits, forcing a choice between specialized connectivity and massive storage. You might be deciding between Credo Technology Group (CRDO -15.20%) and Western Digital (WDC -12.02%) for 2027.

    Credo provides high-speed connectivity solutions that enable artificial intelligence data centers to communicate efficiently, while Western Digital is a global leader in both hard disk and flash storage. While they operate in different niches, both are essential players in the scaling of cloud infrastructure. This comparison evaluates which stock offers the best path for long-term growth.

    Sources indicate that credo Technology Group specializes in high-speed copper and optical interconnect solutions designed for artificial intelligence infrastructure. The company sells products like Active Electrical Cables and optical components to hyperscale operators and system vendors. It has established key partnerships with Oracle (ORCL -8.48%) and Microsoft (MSFT -2.77%) to enhance connectivity for dual-architecture systems.

    The demand for faster semiconductor stocks has significantly boosted its financial performance. In the 12 months ended Aug. 1, 2026, revenue reached nearly $1.6 billion, representing a 165.1% increase over the previous period. This expansion led to a net income of roughly $538.3 million and a net margin of about 33.8%.

    As of its May 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.0x, meaning the organization carries no debt relative to shareholder equity. Its current ratio is approximately 10.2x, indicating a strong ability to cover short-term debts with current assets. In the fiscal year ended May 2, 2026, free cash flow reached nearly $407.0 million, though stock-based compensation represented roughly 39.3% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

    Sources indicate that western Digital designs and supplies essential data-storage solutions for enterprises and hyperscale cloud providers. Its product portfolio includes both hard disk drives and flash-based storage serving a global market across Asia and the Americas. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk, with three individual clients accounting for 16%, 15%, and 13% of total net revenue in its latest annual report.

Net income for this period was nearly $10.0 billion, which indicates a net margin of roughly 69.2%.     #62321. How To Teach Your AI Agent About Your Company

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (790 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    How To Teach Your AI Agent About Your Company

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (790 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Frederik Riskær Pedersen, Founder and CEO of Maplith, a firm brain for your AI agents.
    • For 16 years, I ran a translation company that grew from a handful of people into an international business.
    • Industry observers note that one customer indicates it well.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Frederik Riskær Pedersen, Founder and CEO of Maplith, a firm brain for your AI agents.

    For 16 years, I ran a translation company that grew from a handful of people into an international business. The most important thing I learned about knowledge is that it rarely lives where you think it does.

    Industry observers note that one customer indicates it well. We had to fetch their files from their own system and deliver them in their own layout, and we could only invoice some of the repetitions. None of that was written down anywhere. It lived with one project manager. Anyone else would have done it the standard way and got it wrong.

    That tailoring was not a side issue. It was the product. If the work had been standard, the customer could have run the model themselves. This is why a firm’s rules never get standardized away: The exceptions are often exactly what customers pay for.

    In a recent development, I think of this every time someone asks me why their AI agent isn’t delivering. The models are good enough. The problem is that the agent starts from zero every time. It does not know which systems you run, how they connect or which rules you follow without ever writing them down. So it guesses, and a confident guess in your accounts is worse than no answer at all.

    Here are five things you can do this month before you let an agent work inside your business. None of them needs a latest tool.

    Sources indicate that book two hours with the three or four people who make most of the everyday decisions. Ask them one question: “What would a latest hire ask you in their first week?” The answers are your unwritten rules: which customers get special terms, when a refund is approved, what can be invoiced and what cannot. Write each one as a short sentence, specific enough to check: “This customer gets files back in their own template.” “Refunds above 300 euros are approved by the finance lead.”.

    List every system you use and what each one is the source of truth for. You will find places where two systems describe the same thing differently. “Returned” in the ERP can mean the customer has sent the item back, while in the warehouse it means the item is back on the shelf.

    Industry observers note that the instinct is to make the systems agree. In my experience, that rarely works because each system was set up for the team that uses it, and that is why it works for them. Write the translation down instead. The same goes for numbers. In my company, the price did not sit in the same place from one customer to the next. Note where it lives for whom and which value to trust for which question.

    Sources indicate that most useful answers need two systems joined: the order in the web shop and the invoice in accounting, or the support ticket and the customer in the CRM. Find the field that ties them together and test it by hand. Take 20 random orders and look for them in the other system. If you find 19, you can build on that link. If you find 12, you cannot, and an agent will rarely tell you it is guessing. The test takes an afternoon and saves months of wrong reports.

    Split actions into four levels: read, propose, act after approval and act alone. Start with everything that changes something requiring approval from a named person. Set limits in money and volume, not in trust. When the agent has proposed the same action a hundred times without a mistake, move that one action up a level. That decision should be yours, never the agent’s.

    Recent findings suggest that for every action, record who asked for it, who approved it, what happened and when. It sounds bureaucratic, but it is the only way to answer when a customer, an auditor or your board asks, “Why did this happen?” Without a log, you also cannot tell when it is safe to give the agent more freedom.

    None of this is about artificial intelligence. It is about making knowledge that lives in people’s heads, and in systems that do not talk to each other, available and trustworthy. Companies that do this get more out of their AI. They also become less fragile when a key person goes on holiday or leaves.

    It has been revealed that so start small. Book the two hours this week, write down 10 rules and test one link.

    Sources indicate that forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Few businesses exemplify American business success more than Coca-Cola (KO +0.94%).
    • It has been revealed that over the last 12 months alone, shares have jumped by an impressive 35%, substantially outpacing the S&P 500's return of just 8% over the same time frame.
    • According to recent reports, to understand Coca-Cola's appeal, it can pay to listen to the philosophy of one of its biggest backers, Warren Buffett.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Will Ebiefung – Nov 20, 2026 at 5:05PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Coca-Cola ›.

    Few businesses exemplify American business success more than Coca-Cola (KO +0.94%). Since its founding in the late 19th century, the multinational beverage maker has expanded globally to serve billions and become one of the world's most recognized brands. Investors have profited substantially along the way, and this shows little sign of stopping.

    It has been revealed that over the last 12 months alone, shares have jumped by an impressive 35%, substantially outpacing the S&P 500's return of just 8% over the same time frame. This is a substantial deal for a company that is already large and mature. Let's dig deeper into the pros and cons of Coca-Cola to decide if the company still has millionaire-maker potential.

    NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

    According to recent reports, to understand Coca-Cola's appeal, it can pay to listen to the philosophy of one of its biggest backers, Warren Buffett. His Berkshire Hathaway portfolio owns a whopping $38.4 billion worth of Coca-Cola stock, making it his third-largest bet behind American Express and Apple.

    Buffett likes to invest in companies with simple and easy-to-understand business models that enjoy a strong economic moat. A moat is a competitive advantage that protects a company's market share against competition and allows it to enjoy stable or elevated pricing power. Coca-Cola is arguably the quintessential example of this type of business.

    You can walk into a convenience store or restaurant practically anywhere in the world and find Coca-Cola's flagship beverage Coke (or one of its many subbrands like Sprite, Fanta, and a variety of localized options).

    It has been revealed that the organization's ubiquitous shelf space has created unparalleled habit creation among its consumers, which is something new rivals will struggle to disrupt, even if they manage to create better-tasting products. This advantage also makes Coca-Cola's sales remarkably recession-resistant. It has allowed the company to protect its margins amid soaring global inflation in raw materials like aluminum and sugar.

    Recent findings suggest that coca-Cola's gross margins have hovered around 60%, despite the soaring prices for its products. This suggests the firm is passing on the vast majority of inflation to consumers, while protecting its own profitability.

    KO Gross Profit Margin data by YCharts.

    Coca-Cola isn't without some long-term challenges. The company is already a global brand name, and that means there is very little room for organic growth. Management will be increasingly tempted to rely on price increases to juice investor returns. While the company's gross margin of over 60% was easy to justify back when a 12-pack cost $4.00, it is much harder to stomach when prices have doubled, and more American families are struggling to make ends meet.

    Sources indicate that soda prices have far exceeded the U.S. inflation rate, despite boasting a disproportionately middle- and lower-income consumer base. It's hard not to wonder if this situation is as sustainable as it may look on the surface.

    Over the long term, there could be a generational shift away from brand-name soft drinks as people become more comfortable buying lower-cost store brands from major retailers like Walmart, which offers alternatives like Sam's Cola and Twist Up.

    Coca-Cola's recent performance is impressive, and its strong moat can help set the tech giant up for more market-beating growth over the long term. That stated, with a market cap of $422 billion (in a mature industry with relatively little room for organic growth), Coca-Cola's days of explosive millionaire-making growth are likely behind it. Shares are also somewhat expensive at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple of 28.

    Investors who buy the stock now should look at it as a safer alternative to more speculative opportunities like generative AI. The manufacturer's dividend (currently boasting a yield of 2.21%) will likely represent a sizable percentage of its long-term returns.

    Sources indicate that wembanyama revealed off the "shunk" during the Spurs' 124-112 win over the Los Angeles Clippers on Thursday. The two-time All-Star posted 32 points, 11 rebounds and 1 "shunk.".

    Industry observers note that "I'm not going to lie," Wembanyama mentioned afterward via ESPN. "Actually, I've had this blister forever, and it's killing me. And every time I dunk, it kills me.     Trust Is The Upcoming Battleground For Customer Engagement

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (927 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • James Garvert is the EVP of Fraud & Communications Solutions for TransUnion.
    • ​Engaging with consumers has never been more essential, or more difficult.
    • In a recent development, every interaction depends on trust, yet consumers are more hesitant than ever to engage.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    James Garvert is the EVP of Fraud & Communications Solutions for TransUnion.

    ​Engaging with consumers has never been more essential, or more difficult. Amid the meteoric rise of AI-enabled scams, call spoofing and social engineering attacks, the challenges organizations face when trying to reach consumers seem insurmountable.

    In a recent development, every interaction depends on trust, yet consumers are more hesitant than ever to engage. Many of the traditional warning signs consumers were trained to recognize have disappeared—consumers are on edge.

    And with good reason: It’s a jungle out there.

    Sources indicate that in our recent global study, “61% of business leaders ranked fraud among the risks with the greatest potential business impact, ahead of cybersecurity breaches, compliance, customer churn, operational cost and reputational risk. More concerning, 58% said they’re very or extremely concerned fraud is evolving faster than their organizations’ abilities to detect and prevent it.”.

    Historically, organizations have viewed fraud and engaging with customers as separate disciplines. But today’s threat environment makes it clear they’re deeply interconnected. In many cases, the communication channel itself—whether a phone call, text message, email or mobile app interaction—provides the first indication that fraud may be occurring.

    Industry observers note that consumers don’t experience fraud, identity and communication challenges as separate challenges. To them, it’s one experience, one problem. It’s a trust problem that’s reshaping the customer journey. In fact, 69% of consumers say they would switch vendors for stronger security.

    Trust has become the foundation for both customer engagement and fraud prevention.

    At our recent Fraud & Communications Summit in Chicago, keynote speaker Matt O’Neill, a former U.S. Secret Service Special Agent and recipient of Gold and Silver Awards for distinguished service, shared insights from years spent working undercover as a banker, broker, money launderer and other personas. In these roles, he led multinational investigations into crypto-laundering networks and dark web marketplaces.

    According to O’Neill, fraudsters are winning because fraud has evolved into a highly organized industry. He explained that scam operations now function much like large multinational corporations. Scam compounds are similar to call centers, complete with organizational structures, performance quotas, shift schedules and human resources departments. Unfortunately, many of these compounds operate under sophisticated criminal networks and employ workers who have been trafficked.

    It has been revealed that at the same time, the barrier to entry into the fraud world has never been lower. AI enables fraudsters to create convincing scams at scale in virtually any language, including cloned voices, deepfake videos and personalized social engineering campaigns. And it’s cheap.​.

    In a recent development, the consequences of eroding trust extend well beyond fraud losses. Organizations often experience:.

    • Reduced marketing effectiveness.

    Ironically, the industries and brands most trusted by consumers are frequently among the most targeted by fraudsters, with the highest fraud instances related to auto lending, bank-issued and retail credit cards and unsecured personal lending.

    According to Edelman, trust now rivals price and quality as a primary factor influencing consumer decision-making. Research reveals that “77% of consumers cited confidence their personal data is secure as the most important feature when choosing whom to transact with online.”.

    Organizations can strengthen trust by approaching fraud prevention and customer communications as a unified strategy.

    Recent findings suggest that traditional fraud controls were designed for predictable attacks. Today’s fraudsters adapt quickly, vary their tactics and coordinate attacks across multiple channels and sessions. Identity verification remains key, but it only confirms who someone claims to be. It doesn’t determine whether the current interaction should be trusted.

    Here’s where identity verification falls short:.

    • KYC (Know Your Customer) controls are often strongest at onboarding, not throughout the customer lifecycle.

    • Devices, behaviors and risk profiles change over time.

    • Credentials can be compromised after verification.

    • Synthetic identities can appear legitimate on paper.

    The most important fraud signal is often not a single event. Any single signal can be manipulated or generate false positives. It’s the story that unfolds throughout an interaction. It emerges through relationships among users, devices, accounts, entities and sessions.

    As if it wasn’t hard enough, AI has turbocharged fraud. In addition, labeling identified threats as AI-driven remains a challenge. That’s because it’s difficult to build comprehensive strategies with new AI fraud models evolving so rapidly.

    Recent findings suggest that while fraud practitioners know when an account was taken over, there’s right now no label for how it was taken over and whether AI drove the attack. As a result, the AI-attributed training set doesn’t exist yet for tracking that fraud, and detection stays anchored to heuristics and analyst judgment.

    To be able to engage effectively with consumers and prevent fraud, organizations must adopt continuous authentication and layered risk strategies.

    • Develop a comprehensive strategy—don’t address fraud in silos across your organization.

    • Form strategic partnerships with your cyber teams.

    • Correlate identity, device, behavioral and contextual signals in real time.

    Sources indicate that the process is straightforward: Collect. Correlate. Score. Decide.

    Every phone call, text message, email and digital transaction represents a trust moment. Customers want confidence the organization contacting them is legitimate and their information and transactions are protected. Simply asking consumers to “trust us” is no longer enough.

    Verified identity, authenticated communications and real-time risk intelligence are becoming the foundation of trust in a digital-first world.

    In a recent development, the future isn’t reactive fraud mitigation. It’s proactive trust at the point of interaction, by orchestrating identity, risk and communications intelligence across every customer interaction.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 20, 2026 at 5:15PM EST.
    • Recent findings suggest that pfizer (PFE -0.51%) faces a large patent cliff, and investors worry it won't be able to offset the revenue it loses as older drugs face generic competition.
    • Industry observers note that in fact, revenue from recently launched and acquired drugs rose 32% in the third quarter of 2026.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 20, 2026 at 5:15PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Pfizer ›.

    Recent findings suggest that pfizer (PFE -0.51%) faces a large patent cliff, and investors worry it won't be able to offset the revenue it loses as older drugs face generic competition. That's a problem, but the drugmaker is aware of it and is making important strides in its efforts to address the issue. The major story, however, is that this issue is pretty normal for a drug tech giant.

    Industry observers note that in fact, revenue from recently launched and acquired drugs rose 32% in the third quarter of 2026. That shows the pharmaceutical giant's efforts are bearing fruit. But there's more reason to be excited, including the company's strong balance sheet, its large dividend, and management's commitment to continue paying that dividend. Here's what you need to know.

    One of the biggest worries about Pfizer is its upcoming patent expirations. Two big ones are Eliquis in 2028 and Vyndamax in 2031. But patent expirations are a normal part of the pharma sector. And research and development efforts in the highly technical and intensely competitive healthcare sector don't always align perfectly with a manufacturer's patent expiration schedule. It's just a fact of life.

    Industry observers note that the 32% revenue growth Pfizer achieved from launched and acquired products is evidence that the company is seeing some success in its efforts to address the problem. And it sets up three more reasons to consider buying the stock.

    Sources indicate that pfizer ended the third quarter of 2026 with $1.8 billion in cash and $12.4 billion in short-term investments. That gives the manufacturer significant firepower to support its business through this patent-expiration cycle. In fact, the company's cash hoard is slightly higher than at the start of the year, so it isn't rapidly burning through its savings.

    Despite the firm's results with new drugs and its financial strength, investors are deeply negative on Pfizer's stock. That's highlighted by its huge 6.1% dividend yield as of this writing. To put that yield into context, the S&P 500 index (^GSPC -3.70%) yields roughly 1.1%, and the average pharma stock yields 1.3%.

    It has been revealed that the negativity highlighted by the elevated yield is echoed by more traditional valuation metrics. Pfizer's price-to-sales and price-to-book ratios are below their five-year averages. And while the price-to-earnings ratio is elevated, it is largely due to one-time charges. Looking at the whole picture, Pfizer's stock looks attractively priced.

    NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

    Given the lofty yield, Pfizer is likely to be most appealing to dividend-focused investors. But right now earnings aren't covering the dividend. That's not a great sign, but one-time charges are part of the matter. If you look at cash flow, the company can still support the dividend. That's highlighted by a cash dividend payout ratio of roughly 85%. While a lower number would be better, there's still some room for adversity. And don't forget about the company's large cash pile.

    Both of these facts help support management's strong backing of the dividend. Indeed, one of Pfizer's key capital priorities is to "maintain and grow our dividend." Obviously, the company's priorities could change, but it wouldn't make a statement like that if the board of directors wasn't on board with protecting the dividend.

    At the end of the day, Pfizer is facing very real headwinds today. But it is an industry-leading firm with a long history of success. If history is any guide, it will muddle through this difficult period. The success it is having with fresh drugs, its financial strength, attractive valuation, and dedication to its large dividend are all strong reasons for investors to take a deep dive before 2026 is over. If you wait too long, the opportunity here may pass you by.

    • According to recent reports, in his first season with the Patriots, Brown has already missed six of the team's 10 games.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    New England Patriots receiver A.J. Brown is expected to be sidelined for multiple weeks due to a hamstring injury, according to ESPN's Mike Reiss and Adam Schefter.

    Brown, 29, injured his hamstring during Week 10's 35-10 loss to the Detroit Lions in Munich. He got hurt in the fourth quarter and did not return, finishing with two catches (on six targets) for 27 yards.

    According to recent reports, in his first season with the Patriots, Brown has already missed six of the team's 10 games. First, he sustained a high ankle sprain in the season opener and sat out four games while on injured reserve. Then he was sidelined for an additional two games due to a strained knee.

    The news on Brown comes as the Patriots also officially announced that quarterback Drake Maye suffered a fractured right fibula against the Lions and could miss the remainder of the regular season.

    Latest England dropped to 5-5 following the defeat versus Detroit and has lost three of its past four games. The Patriots have a bye for Week 11, then visit the Los Angeles Chargers (1-8) in Week 12. New England is still in the AFC playoff race, just one game behind the Cleveland Browns (6-4) for the conference's third wild-card berth.

    In a recent development, with Brown injured, the Patriots' receiver depth chart consists of Mack Hollins, DeMario Douglas, Efton Chism III and Kyle Williams. Romeo Doubs could join them after the bye week when he's eligible to be activated from IR. Douglas is the team's leading pass-catcher among wideouts with 32 receptions for 438 yards and four touchdowns.

    Brown was acquired from the Philadelphia Eagles during the offseason, trading a 2028 first-round pick and 2027 fifth-round selection. He registered 1,003 receiving yards last season with the Eagles (his lowest total in four seasons). However, Brown had reportedly become frustrated with quarterback Jalen Hurts — and his role in the Eagles' offense.

    Philadelphia traded Brown before a three-year, $96 million extension kicked in that takes him through the 2029 season.

    According to recent reports, brown is in his eighth NFL season, beginning his career with the Tennessee Titans. He was the team's second-round selection (No. 51 overall) out of Ole Miss and played with the team for three seasons.

    Industry observers note that the 6-foot-1 receiver was dealt to the Eagles during the 2022 NFL Draft for first- and fourth-round picks. He subsequently received a four-year, $100 million extension from Philadelphia.

    A three-time Pro Bowler and two-time second-team All-Pro selection, Brown has 535 career receptions for 8,157 yards and 56 touchdowns.

    Neocloud tech giant CoreWeave (CRWV) is benefiting from robust AI-driven demand for cloud computing.

    Sources indicate that recently, JPMorgan analyst Samik Chatterjee upgraded CoreWeave to buy from hold, raising his price target to $125 from $120. The analyst cited favorable pricing, driven by solid demand, for the upgrade.

    Chatterjee said CoreWeave is now more willing to sign premium priced, shorter-term contracts, which lift his revenue and margin estimates. CRWV stock performance has been underwhelming as investors worry about high capital spending, the analyst noted. That said, he believes that higher prices and increased margins will more than offset the rise in debt to fund capital spending, improving the stock's valuation.

    Chatterjee noted the 25% price hike in July across CoreWeave's product offerings and frequent price increases by rivals like Nebius (NBIS), adding that some peers are charging nearly three times more for short-term compute contracts than what CoreWeave charges on longer-term deals.

    It has been revealed that "CoreWeave's leverage of the opportunity [is] evident in its recent press release highlighting contracts signed in F3Q at ~$40M/MW," remarked Chatterjee. JPMorgan said higher pricing is already contributing 5-10 percentage points to contract margins versus earlier deals.

    Industry observers note that chatterjee ranks No. 4 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 75% of the time, delivering an average return of 55.3%. See CoreWeave Statistics on TipRanks.

    Sources indicate that palo Alto Networks (PANW) is a provider of cybersecurity solutions across network, cloud, security operations, AI and identity. Following a discussion with management, BTIG analyst Gray Powell reiterated a buy rating on PANW and raised his price target to $425 from $404.

    After a review of Palo Alto's product-level growth catalysts, Powell sees clear upside to both revenue and next-generation security (NGS) annual recurring revenue (ARR) in fiscal 2027. He expects PANW to deliver pro forma revenue growth of more than 17%, above the consensus estimate of 14.6%, and NGS ARR growth of more than 26% versus the Street's expectation of 24.5%.

    Over the past five years, the Palo Alto business mix, has moved to higher-growth product areas and newly introduced markets. from what was earlier viewed as a hardware-centric network security organization, Powell said. The 5-star analyst estimates that hardware firewalls and attached subscriptions now account for less than 50% of revenue.

    In a recent development, meanwhile, high-growth solutions, including Prisma SASE, software firewalls, Cortex XSIAM, Chronosphere and Idira now represent more than 35% of PANW's revenue. "Investors may not fully realize the growth potential within PANW's platform story," Powell mentioned.

    BTIG is optimistic about the prospects of Chronosphere in observability, CyberArk in identity and software firewalls and Prisma AIRS in the network and AI security business.

    Sources indicate that powell ranks No. 320 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 17.3%. See Palo Alto Networks KPIs on TipRanks.

    According to recent reports, in a research note on September 30, Rosenblatt analyst Scott Devitt reiterated a buy rating on e-commerce and cloud computing platform Amazon (AMZN), raising his price target to $360 from $335. Fears that agentic commerce poses a major threat to Amazon's advertising business seem "overstated," he said.

    Devitt noted that the growing adoption of personal agents and AI shopping assistants has sparked concern about displacement of Amazon's retail media business. But the 5-star analyst remains bullish, given Amazon's ability to adapt to changing consumer behavior, as it's done in the past.

    It has been revealed that additionally, Devitt argues that even if an AI agent helps a shopper discover a product, Amazon can still handle the purchase and delivery, keeping much of the transaction value. He highlighted that management believes that existing Amazon shoppers will likely continue to start their shopping journey on the platform because it has better personalization, accurate pricing and inventory information that third-party agents still lack.

    Recent findings suggest that overall, Devitt expects Amazon's retail business to prove a net beneficiary of agentic commerce. Fewer clicks would not hurt the company if the value of each remaining click and overall volumes keep rising, he said. The argument is that even if Amazon loses some sponsored ad revenue over the next few years, it would likely be only a small part of the company's total business and could be offset by growth in other areas.

    It has been revealed that "Consistent with our AI framework, we continue to view Amazon as one of the most resilient leaders in our coverage, combining owned compute infrastructure with a physical fulfillment moat," said Devitt. His bullish view is supported, Devitt said, by expectations that Amazon Web Services (AWS) will exit the year at a more than 45% growth rate with continued margin improvement.
